description: e are a trio of friends fascinated by planetary science, deep-space exploration, and the future of human life on Mars. For this year’s NASA Space Apps Challenge, we are diving into the Interplanetary Survival Guide: Martian Map challenge. Driven by pure curiosity and a love for turning complex space data into clear visual stories, we want to imagine what the ultimate navigation guide looks like for the first astronauts walking on the Red Planet.
summary:
Ares Sozon is an interactive Mars surface-planning tool for astronauts. It combines a 3D globe, a flat map with a directory of named places, and a simulated ground view built from NASA MOLA elevation data and Mars imagery. A single click on any spot gives a survival scorecard (terrain slope, radiation shielding and sunlight); a double-click drops into a ground-level view of that location.

 To address the challenge, we built a planet-wide route planner that finds the safest path between two points, shows alternative routes with their risks, and warns about steep slopes and hazards. Layer modes cover safety, resources, hazards and imagery. A stranded-astronaut tool finds the nearest reachable shelter within an oxygen limit, accounting for slope-slowed walking in a spacesuit. A Missions mode adds simulated astronaut briefings.

 Elevation, slope and imagery are real NASA/USGS data, plus a real radiation patch over Arcadia. Ice, sunlight and dust risk are clearly labelled as derived estimates, not measurements.

 It matters because crews landing on unfamiliar terrain must weigh safety, radiation and oxygen before they move. Ares Sozon puts those decisions in one clear, explorable map and shows where the data is still missing.
details:
What it does and how it works

Ares Sozon is a Mars map built for one question: is it safe to go there? You spin a 3D globe of Mars and click anywhere to get a survival scorecard that rates the spot on terrain slope, radiation shielding and sunlight. Double-click, and you drop to ground level, in a view drawn from NASA's MOLA elevation data. There's also a flat map with a directory of named places. A route planner works like a map app for a whole planet. You choose a start and a goal, and it finds the safest path, shows alternatives with their risks and warns you about steep ground. If an astronaut is stranded, the app finds the nearest shelter they can actually reach on the oxygen they have, because walking slows down on slopes.

Benefits

Instead of juggling separate datasets, a crew or a planner gets terrain, radiation, sunlight and hazards in one place. They can compare sites and routes in seconds, and see what a walk will cost in oxygen before anyone commits to it. It runs in an ordinary browser, and it also works offline from a folder, which helps when the connection is bad or missing.

Intended impact

We want Mars safety planning to be easier to understand, whether you're a mission planner, a student or just curious. It's a prototype and says so on the card, not mission advice. What we hope it shows is how real elevation and slope data can become a safety decision, and that it's honest about which numbers are measured and which are estimated.

Tools, languages, hardware and software

The app is plain HTML, JavaScript and canvas, with no outside libraries. We prepared the data with Python, using NumPy, Pillow and rasterio, from NASA and USGS elevation and imagery files. We built it on a Windows PC, ran it locally with Python's built-in web server, and deployed it on Cloudflare Pages using Node.js and Wrangler. We wrote the code with help from Claude, an AI assistant made by Anthropic.

Creativity

The part we like most is how smoothly you go from the whole planet to the ground: one click for the scorecard, a double-click to land. The stranded-astronaut tool turns "can they walk to safety on the oxygen they have?" into something you can see on a map. Missions mode adds simulated astronaut briefings, so the data reads more like a mission than a spreadsheet.

Factors we considered

Astronaut safety came first, and it shaped the scorecard, the hazard warnings and the oxygen limit. We were careful about honesty: elevation, slope and imagery are real NASA and USGS data, along with a real radiation patch over Arcadia, while ice, sunlight and dust risk are labelled as estimates. We also thought about spacesuit mobility, so walking speed drops on slopes, and about how easy it is to use, with plain clicks and readable cards. Finally, we made a lighter-resolution version of the terrain so the hosted app fits on free hosting, and kept the full-detail version for offline use.
